title: Lineare Separierbarkeit in tiefen neuronalen Netzen — Interaktive Erkundung
category_reason: It is a German interactive explainer of a deep-learning paper (Zhang et al., arXiv:2307.13962, 2023) that measures per-layer linear separability of hidden-layer activations in deep neural networks and uses it to explain why larger nets generalize; the whole content is about neural nets, training, and generalization.
thesis: An interactive German walkthrough of Zhang et al. (arXiv:2307.13962, 2023): the paper asks whether the internal work of a deep network can be measured layer by layer, and answers yes by defining a geometric 'linear separability' (LS) of each hidden layer's activations, showing that training and separability rise in lockstep ('synchronicity'), and using random-matrix bounds to explain why deeper and wider nets generalize better even though classical VC/Rademacher theory predicts overfitting.
key_claims: The motivating gap: classical complexity theory (VC dimension, Rademacher) says large nets overfit, but practice shows large nets generalize better; the paper proposes a simple per-layer geometric measure — how well a hyperplane separates the two class clouds of a layer's activations.

Theorem 3: two sets A, B are linearly separable iff every point of the Minkowski difference MD(A,B) = {a_i - b_j} lies on one side of a hyperplane through the origin; the Minkowski-difference trick reduces 'two clouds, one separating line' to 'one cloud, one hyperplane through the origin'.

The MD-LSM gives four numeric LS measures: LS* (fraction of MD-points on the better side; NP-hard to optimize), LS_1 (ratio of absolute distances, in (0,1], 1 = perfectly separable), and LS_2 (squared; rewrites as a generalized eigenvalue problem with a closed, efficiently solvable form — the reason it is usable in practice); a cheap approximation sets MM^T = I so omega_hat = m_tilde/||m_tilde|| is just a sum, no eigendecomposition.

Theorem 1 (synchronicity): whenever training raises the training accuracy in an epoch, the linear separability of the hidden layer rises in the same epoch, and conversely; the per-layer LS curves track the accuracy curve, with deeper layers (closer to the output) showing higher LS.
Theorem 9: a purely linear transformation cannot change separability (only rotation/stretch); it is the non-linear activation that lets a net reorder the points and 'untangle' the classes.
Theorem 11: if F_sigma(x,y) > 2 then the activation moves MD-points from the minor side to the major side, i.e. it increases separability; sigmoid, tanh, arctan, and softsign all satisfy this.

Theorem 12 / Corollary 13 (random-matrix bounds): the probability that separability increases rises with width H (term H * exp(-LS_2^2 / 8 sigma^2) is linear in H but then dominated by the exponential once LS_2 is already high), so a wider or deeper net has a higher chance of increasing LS — the structural explanation for why bigger nets need not overfit.
Best linear classification accuracy is always >= LS* (Theorem 7), and all four measures are monotone in separability; the four measures are validated empirically on MLPs, CNNs, ResNets and ViTs.

Minkowski (Minkowski-set) difference MD(A,B) = {a_i - b_j}

a draw-your-own-points linear-separability lab: add class A / class B points, rotate the separating line and shift the bias, with live accuracy and a separable/not-separable verdict
a side-by-side original-vs-Minkowski-difference panel with a rotatable separating hyperplane through the origin and config presets (separable / overlapping / XOR-like)

internal_tensions: Theory-vs-practice is the driving tension: classical generalization bounds predict overfitting for large nets, while the paper's structural separability argument says size helps; the piece leans on the latter to close the gap.
LS* is the most intuitive measure but NP-hard to optimize, so the practically useful LS_2 relies on the MM^T = I approximation — a deliberate loss of exactness for speed that the paper flags.
It is a visualization/interpretation piece, not a proof: the deep theorems are asserted and illustrated, and the claims are validated empirically rather than derived end-to-end here.

title: Kants Kritik der reinen Vernunft – Interaktiv
category_reason: It is a German interactive companion to Kant's Critique of Pure Reason, covering the architecture of the Critique, the Copernican turn, space and time as forms of intuition, the categories, analytic/synthetic judgments, appearance vs thing-in-itself, and the transcendental dialectic; it is a philosophy-of-mind/epistemology piece with no ML/neural-net focus.
thesis: An interactive German companion to Kant's Critique of Pure Reason: it asks 'what can we know at all?', turns the inquiry from the world to the faculties of cognition themselves, and stages each core idea — the Copernican reversal, space/time as a priori forms of intuition, the categories of the understanding, the analytic/synthetic distinction, appearance vs. thing-in-itself, and the transcendental dialectic — as a clickable Canvas demo.
key_claims: The Critique is a map of our thinking: it does not investigate the world but the cognitive faculty, showing where secure knowledge is possible and where we drift into illusion.

The Copernican turn: it is not our knowledge that conforms to objects but objects that conform to our knowledge; like Copernicus rotating the observer instead of the stars, Kant reverses the subject-object relation (pre-Kant dogmatism = the mind as a passive mirror of reality).
Space and time are not properties of things-in-themselves but a priori forms of our intuition — the 'glasses' through which all experience is possible; they precede experience and make it possible.
The categories of the understanding are the a priori concepts the mind applies to synthesize the manifold of intuition into objects of experience.
Judgments split into analytic (predicate contained in subject) and synthetic (predicate adds something); Kant's project is to explain how synthetic a priori judgments (e.g. mathematics) are possible.
The distinction between appearance (phenomena, things as they appear to us) and the thing-in-itself (noumenon, the thing independent of our cognition) is the backbone of the system.
The transcendental dialectic shows how reason, when it goes beyond possible experience, falls into illusions/antinomies (the famous contradictory demands about the world as a whole).
visualizations: a tabbed (nav-button) interactive layout with eight sections, each an annotated Canvas 2D diagram plus controls
an overview diagram of the architecture of the Critique with animated build-up and clickable elements
a 'Copernican revolution' slider that rotates the perspective from pre-Kant (mind mirrors world) to post-Kant (world conforms to mind)
a space-and-time demo with toggles to turn the forms of intuition 'on/off' and see what happens to experience
a categories diagram, an analytic/synthetic-judgment demo, an appearance-vs-thing-in-itself diagram, and a transcendental-dialectic diagram
a closing self-test quiz
internal_tensions: The appearance/thing-in-itself split is the load-bearing tension: the mind can know phenomena but never the noumenon, so the very framework that makes knowledge possible also limits it.
The Copernican turn is presented as the fix for dogmatism, but it is itself a radical, hard-to-justify move (objects conforming to the knowing subject), which the piece stages rather than defends.
No AI/ML content; this is a pedagogical philosophy piece, and its demos are illustrative diagrams rather than rigorous reconstructions of Kant's arguments.

title: Attention ist Optimaler Transport — Einfach erklärt
category_reason: It is a German interactive explainer of a 2025 deep-learning theory paper (Litman, Stanford, arXiv:2508.08369) that derives softmax attention from one-sided entropic optimal transport and shows backprop through attention is a REINFORCE policy-gradient; it is squarely about transformer attention and learning.
thesis: An interactive German 'simple' version of Litman (Stanford, 2025, arXiv:2508.08369), 'Scaled-Dot-Product Attention as One-Sided Entropic Optimal Transport': softmax attention, invented in 2017 by intuition, is shown to be the UNIQUE solution of a clean optimization problem — maximize similarity while staying maximally undecisive while being a probability — and, more surprisingly, the gradient used to learn attention is a REINFORCE policy-gradient whose variance-reducing baseline falls out for free; the two routes (optimal transport and RL) are then shown to be the same object via the Fisher matrix.
key_claims: Softmax is a choice made in 2017 that simply worked; the paper's point is that softmax is not a design choice but the unique solution of a well-posed problem on the simplex (maximize similarity, stay maximally undecisive, be a probability).

The decisive trick: classical optimal transport fixes both marginals (a source pile and a target pile, solved by Sinkhorn iteration); here only ONE side is fixed — a single source (one Dirac = one 'quantum of attention') with a free target — so the plan matrix collapses to a single row vector and the feasible region is exactly the simplex, giving a closed-form solution with no iteration (this is the distinction from 'Sinkhorn attention').

Theorem 3.3 (exists / unique / form): the objective J(p) = -<p, s> + tau * sum p_j log p_j over the simplex attains a minimum (extreme-value theorem), the minimum is unique (linear <p,s> plus the strictly convex entropy term make J strictly convex), and Lagrange/KKT stationarity gives p_j proportional to exp(s_j / tau), i.e. exactly softmax.

Remark 3.4 (why tau = sqrt(d_k)): if q and k have independent mean-0 variance-1 components then <q,k> has variance d_k; dividing by sqrt(d_k) rescales the variance back to 1, otherwise softmax saturates to one-hot and the gradients vanish — the division is a variance normalization / a matching of the entropic-regularization strength to the dimension.

One regularizer, many mechanisms: argmin_p -<p,s> + Omega(p) over the simplex; swapping Omega gives softmax (Omega = -tau H, dense), sparsemax (Omega = 1/2 sum p_j^2, exact zeros via L2 projection), alpha-entmax (Tsallis, continuously tunable sparsity), and ALiBi (Omega = -tau H + gamma sum p_j |i-j|, a linear distance penalty / local bias).

Theorem 5.2 (the backpass = REINFORCE): with context c(p) = sum p_j v_j, utility u_j = -dL/dp_j and advantage A_j = u_j - E_p[u], the gradient is dL/ds_j = -(p_j*/tau)(u_j - E_p[u]) = -(p_j*/tau) A_j — literally REINFORCE with an expectation baseline; the baseline is a free gift because the softmax Jacobian (1/tau) p_k (delta_kj - p_j) has column sum 0, a pure consequence of sum p_j = 1, which makes the gradient low-variance and training stable.

Theorem 6.3 (the dual potential): minimizing J yields the dual potential phi*(s) = tau log(sum_j exp(s_j/tau)) = Log-Sum-Exp, with the three identities phi* = -V, grad phi* = p*, and Hessian phi* = tau F(s) — the value, gradient and curvature of a single scalar encode the problem, the solution and the learning dynamics.

Corollary 7.5 (the 'ring closure'): d2/ds2 phi*(s) = tau F(s) = (1/tau)(diag(p*) - p*(p*)^T) — the curvature of the dual potential equals (up to tau) the Fisher information matrix equals the RL 'transducer'; three perspectives (optimal transport, information geometry, reinforcement learning) land on the same one matrix, which acts as a 'gearbox' damping the learning signal where the strategy has already decided (at the simplex boundary) — manifold-aware learning.

Honesty section: no new mechanism (SDPA is bit-for-bit identical), no experiments (a purely theoretical paper), and the max-entropy/Gibbs link is classical (Jaynes 1957); what is new is the one-sided entropic-OT embedding (closed form, no Sinkhorn), the policy-gradient bridge (baseline for free), and the geometric explanation of why they belong together (Corollary 7.5).

visualizations: a 'touch it first' attention demo: five key words in a circle, a draggable query arrow in the centre, with the attention 'wandering' and a temperature slider (narrow/safe vs broad/open) and winner-key / entropy readouts (2D Canvas)

a one-sided transport animation stepping full OT (two marginals, square) -> single Dirac source -> drop the column condition -> one row = simplex
a live optimizer demo: a mirror-descent numerical solver rolling into the valley of J, racing the analytic softmax (star); the gap between them goes to zero as scores/temperature change
a family-comparison plot: same scores, four distributions (softmax / sparsemax / entmax / ALiBi) with alpha and gamma sliders and non-zero-entry / entropy readouts
an 'attention bandit' (2D Canvas): rows for strategy p, utility u, advantage A and the update Delta s; E[u] climbs monotonically to the best arm as the policy gradient runs

a Fisher-matrix-as-gearbox plot: an 'enthusiasm' (score sharpness) slider showing edge damping where p is concentrated
a six-question self-test quiz with a live score
internal_tensions: The tension between 'it was a lucky 2017 guess' and 'it is forced by mathematics' — the piece's entire point is that the guess is actually the unique optimum, which it proves via strict convexity rather than by re-inventing anything.

One-sided vs full optimal transport: dropping the second marginal is what turns an intractable (Sinkhorn-iterated) problem into a closed-form one; the piece is careful to mark this as the real novelty and to avoid conflating it with existing Sinkhorn-attention work.

It is purely theoretical with no experiments, so all 'results' are identities and geometric explanations of an already-shipped mechanism (SDPA), not performance gains — the piece states this explicitly as a boundary of the claim.

title: Ologs – Interaktive Reise durch Spivak & Kent (2012)
category_reason: It is a German interactive companion to Spivak & Kent (2012), 'Ologs: A Categorical Framework for Knowledge Representation'; although knowledge representation is a classical AI sub-field, the content here is pure categorical logic (categories, functors, limits, database schemas) with no ML/neural-net component.
thesis: An interactive German journey through Spivak & Kent (2012), 'Ologs: A Categorical Framework for Knowledge Representation': it argues that scientific and corporate knowledge is trapped in 'silos' of prose that cannot be precisely linked, and that ologs — labelled categories / sketches — give a language that is both human-readable and machine-precise, serving as database schemas, expressing primitive recursion, and being composable between authors via functors.
key_claims: The problem ologs solve: knowledge is stored in prose 'silos' that cannot be precisely linked; we need a language that is human-readable AND machine-precise and can translate ideas between different authors.

The idea is to use the language of category theory: boxes for concepts (types), arrows for functional relations (aspects), and commutative diagrams for facts; a basic olog is exactly a category with English labels, where each element has a meaning.
An olog-arrow IS a function between sets: every source element has exactly one arrow out, no source may point at two targets (no ambiguity), but two sources may point at the same target.

Categories = graphs plus path-equivalences: arrows compose, and two different paths A -> C may be declared equal (a commutative diagram); this is what 'pins down' meaning and is the key difference from RDF/OWL/semantic nets.

Building blocks: a Type is a box labelled with a noun ('a person', 'a woman', 'a pair (a,b) where ...'); an Aspect is an arrow = function ('a woman is a person'); a Fact is a commutative diagram ('the female parent of a person is their mother' = two paths are equivalent); good style has boxes start with 'a/an' and arrows form English sentences.
Instances: ologs double as database schemas — a schema (the olog) and a set of instances (a model/functor into Set) are cleanly separated, and primitive recursion can be expressed.

Functors connect ologs (e.g. products, pullbacks, coproducts, pushouts), letting one knowledge model be translated into another and composed, which is what makes them more composable than RDF/OWL/semantic nets in precision.

It is explicitly positioned against RDF/OWL/semantic nets as more precise and composable, but that is a comparative claim about expressivity/compositionality, not an empirical one — the value is structural, and the piece is a categorical-logic tutorial rather than a KR system.
Though knowledge representation is a long-standing AI sub-field, this particular artefact has no learning/neural content; the 'AI' is classical symbolic/compositional knowledge modelling.

title: Warum fühlt sich Raum so an? - Interaktive Erklärung

key_claims: The central question is reframed from 'why do we see certain objects' to 'why does the extended canvas itself feel extended' — spatial experience is modelled as a 'painting' whose surface, not just its content, is what we feel.

Space is the right place to start (rather than, e.g., colour) because it is introspectively decomposable (has internal structure), is universal (visual + bodily + ...), and is scientifically accessible.

title: Kohärente Welt — Garben, Keime, Situs
category_reason: It is a German slide-deck (arrow-key presentation) that builds sheaf/germ/situs and infinity-coherence theory from the ground up (point -> neighborhood -> measurement -> stalk -> germ -> gluing -> situs -> limits); it is pure math (sheaf and infinity-category theory) with no ML/neural-net focus.
thesis: A German slide-deck, 'Kohärente Welt' (a coherent world), that reconstructs the sheaf-theoretic worldview step by step: from a single point, to a neighborhood (without distance), to a measurement (thermometer -> number), to a stalk (many measurements at one point), to germs (behaviour in arbitrarily small neighbourhoods), to compatibility/incompatibility on overlaps (where incompatibility is glossed as measurement error, wrong model, lie, or 'hallucination'), to the presheaf -> sheaf gluing condition, to an infinity-sheaf / infinity-coherence upgrade, and finally to situs and limits.
key_claims: The whole sheaf-theoretic vocabulary can be built up from a single point: a point, then a neighbourhood (a notion of 'near' without any metric/distance), then a measurement (a thermometer that turns a point into a number).

Many measurements at the same point (temperature, colour, tone, humidity, pressure, ...) bundle into a stalk (Halm); a germ (Keim) is the behaviour of a local section in arbitrarily small neighbourhoods of a point.

On overlapping neighbourhoods, two local sections are compatible iff their restrictions agree on the overlap (s_1|_{U intersect V} = s_2|_{U intersect V}); when they disagree (s_1| != s_2|) that signals a measurement error, a wrong model, a different object, a lie, or a 'hallucination'.
The presheaf -> sheaf step is the gluing condition: compatible local sections glue to a single global section; a sheaf is exactly the data where local information coheres into global information.

The 'Blitz und Donner' (lightning and thunder) slide exposes the subtlety: two stalks with the same origin that are NOT equal on the time axis; they are reconciled by an equalizer (f(x) = g(y), e.g. t_Ton = t_Blitz + d/v_Schall), so the stalks are 'homotopic' (connected by a reversible transformation).

The infinity-sheaf / infinity-coherence (infinite-Koherenz) step generalizes the classical sheaf gluing to higher coherences, and the deck closes by moving to situs and to limits — the abstract, category-theoretic form of 'a coherent world'.

internal_tensions: The load-bearing tension is coherence-vs-truth: compatible local data glues into a global object (coherence), but coherence is explicitly NOT truth — the deck carries a dedicated 'coherent but not true' slide to keep the two apart.

Incompatibility on overlaps is the flashpoint: the same mathematical condition (disagreement on the overlap) is glossed in many different ways (measurement error, wrong model, different object, lie, hallucination), which is a deliberate interpretive stretch from pure sheaf theory.

The leap from classical sheaves to infinity-sheaves / situs / limits is the big conceptual jump; the deck presents it as a natural upgrade, but it is the move from a set-valued gluing condition to higher-categorical coherence.

title: Grokking Experiments — What They Actually Did
category_reason: It is an English interactive breakdown of the deep-learning 'grokking' experiments (Power et al., 2021) in which a tiny transformer learns binary operation tables and later generalizes; it is squarely about neural-network training and generalization.
thesis: An interactive English reconstruction of exactly what Power et al. (2021), 'Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets', experimented with: a tiny overparameterized transformer (~400K params) learns binary operation tables over abstract symbols, and the piece walks through seven experiments to show which operations generalize, what makes generalization happen (weight decay + noise), the dramatic memorization-then-grokking gap (double descent), robustness to wrong labels, the geometric structure learned inside (t-SNE of embeddings), and a hidden isomorphism between different operations.
key_claims: The setup: a decoder-only transformer (2 layers, width 128, 4 heads, ~400K non-embedding params) trained on 5 tokens <a> <op> <b> = <c> with loss only on the answer token c, where each element is an ABSTRACT SYMBOL (no numeric structure given), AdamW lr=1e-3 weight-decay=1, batch 512, 10^5-step budget — massively overparameterized, so classical theory predicts mere memorization.

Experiment 1 (which operations generalize): symmetric operations (x+y, x^2+y^2) need less data than asymmetric ones (x-y, x/y); x+y mod (p-1) and x*y mod p are mathematically equivalent via primitive roots and indeed show identical curves; some operations (e.g. x^3 + x y^2 + y) never generalize even at 95% data; and mixed operations (divide if odd, subtract if even) CAN generalize — the network learns to dispatch.

Experiment 2 (ablations on the S_5 group product, 120 elements / 14400 equations): weight decay is 'king' and roughly halves the data needed; weight decay toward the origin beats decay toward the initialization; any source of noise (mini-batch SGD, gradient noise, weight noise) helps, consistent with 'noise finds flatter minima'; the learning rate must be within ~1 order of magnitude; and ALL configurations reach 100% training accuracy in 10^3-10^4 steps, so generalization — not optimization — is the bottleneck.

thesis: A German interactive, geometry-first explanation of the attention mechanism in 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al., 2017): attention is content-dependent routing — each token sends a query into the embedding space, matches it against other tokens' keys (similarity = dot product / projected length), normalizes to weights with softmax, and outputs a convex combination of the values; the Q/K/V matrices cut slanted subspaces to specialize the comparison, and multi-head attention runs several such 'views' in parallel.

W^Q, W^K, W^V cut slanted 64-dim subspaces out of the full 512-dim embedding space, giving specialized views: the query space ('what am I looking for?'), the key space ('what do I offer?'), and the value space ('what do I pass on?'); they are oblique projections, not axis-aligned slices, so different aspects (syntax / semantics / position) can be emphasised.

Q * K is the dot product, geometrically the projected length of one vector onto the other: same direction -> large positive score -> high attention; perpendicular -> ~0; opposite -> negative -> ~0 after softmax.
Division by sqrt(d_k) (here sqrt(64) = 8) normalizes the dot-product variance (which is ~d_k in 64 dims) back to ~1; without it softmax saturates and the gradients vanish.

Softmax turns the scaled scores into a probability distribution (all positive, sum to 1); temperature controls sharpness — low temperature = one token dominates (near a hard lookup), high temperature = near-uniform.

Multi-head attention cuts 8 different 64-dim subspaces (each with its own W^Q, W^K, W^V), each attending to a different aspect (syntax / semantics / local / verb-noun / reference / position / negation / long-range); the 8 outputs (64d each) are concatenated (to 512d) and projected back by W^O.
